Safe.label: Safe to delete
Safe.meaning: Known cache, temp, or leftover. No user data. Rebuilds itself.

ProbablySafe.label: Probably safe
ProbablySafe.meaning: Rebuildable or recoverable, but a bigger consequence if wrong.

UserCall.label: Needs your call
UserCall.meaning: Could be personal data. Review before deciding.

Suspicious.label: Suspicious
Suspicious.meaning: Looks wrong â€” known bug or abnormal size. Investigate.

rules.reason: Windows user temp files. Apps recreate them as needed.
rules.article: Temp files are the working scratch of Windows. Clearing them is safe; anything deleted gets regenerated when an app needs it.

rules.reason: Windows system temp files. Recreated on demand.
rules.article: System-wide temp directory. Safe to clear; Windows regenerates what it needs.

rules.reason: Windows Update download cache. Redownloaded if needed.
rules.article: Windows Update stores downloads here before installing them. If deleted, Windows re-downloads only what's still needed.

rules.reason: Kernel crash dump from a previous BSOD. Only useful for diagnosing a crash.
rules.article: Written when Windows itself crashes. Unless Microsoft support asked you to keep it, safe to delete.

rules.reason: Live kernel diagnostic reports.
rules.article: Diagnostic dumps written when a driver crashes but doesn't take the system down. Safe to clear.

rules.reason: Python package cache. Rebuilds on next pip install.
rules.article: pip stores downloaded wheels here. Clearing it just means the next install re-downloads.

rules.reason: npm package cache. Rebuilds on next npm install.
rules.article: Same as pip cache, but for Node.js.

rules.reason: Gradle build cache. Rebuilds on next Android/Gradle build.
rules.article: Used when building Android apps. Safe to clear; the next build re-downloads dependencies.

rules.reason: Maven repository cache. Rebuilds on next Maven build.
rules.article: Java dependency cache. Same pattern as Gradle.

rules.reason: Leftover from BlueStacks. Only delete after uninstalling BlueStacks.
rules.article: BlueStacks (Android emulator) stores its engine disks here. After uninstalling BlueStacks, this folder is orphaned and safe to remove.

rules.reason: Google Play Games emulator data. Only delete after uninstalling Play Games.
rules.article: Play Games is a buggy emulator that grows without bound. After uninstalling, this folder is orphaned.

rules.reason: Known Google Play Games bug: this file grows without bound. Reports hundreds of GB but is often sparse on disk.
rules.article: Google Play Games' userdata.img is a well-documented bug. It balloons to hundreds of GB, often much larger than any real data. If Play Games is uninstalled, this file is dead weight.

rules.reason: Docker's virtual disk. Prune inside Docker first, then compact.
rules.article: Docker stores all images and containers here. 'docker system prune -a' frees unused ones, then the VHDX can be compacted.

rules.reason: WSL distro disks. Deleting loses the Linux environment. Compact instead to shrink.
rules.article: Each WSL distro is a VHDX that grows but never shrinks. Compact with Optimize-VHD or diskpart to reclaim space without deleting your environment.

rules.reason: Android emulator images. Recreate via Android Studio â†’ Device Manager.
rules.article: Each AVD is a full Android system image, typically 3-10 GB each. Safe to delete unused ones; Android Studio can recreate them on demand.

rules.reason: Android system images for the emulator. Re-downloadable via SDK Manager.
rules.article: One system image per Android API level. Keep only the levels you actually test on.

rules.reason: Claude Desktop's local VM bundle. Best removed by uninstall + reinstall.
rules.article: Claude Desktop runs a local VM for some features. This folder is large but deleting it directly may break the app. Uninstall + reinstall Claude Desktop to remove cleanly.

rules.reason: Hibernation file. If you don't use hibernate/sleep, disable with 'powercfg /h off' (admin).
rules.article: Takes 40% of your RAM size. Removing it means hibernate and Fast Startup stop working, but normal shutdown/restart still work.

rules.reason: Synced to cloud. Use 'Free up space' in OneDrive settings to make files online-only instead of deleting.
rules.article: OneDrive keeps local copies of cloud files. If space is tight, right-click tray â†’ Free up space â€” this converts them to online-only placeholders without losing anything.

rules.reason: Your downloads. Review contents before removing.
rules.article: Downloads can contain anything from installers to personal files. Check the top items before deciding.

rules.reason: Your personal documents.
rules.article: Personal files. Review before deleting anything in here.

rules.reason: Your videos.
rules.article: Video files are large but irreplaceable. Back up, don't delete.

rules.reason: Custom folder in your profile. Inspect before deciding.
rules.article: Not a recognized system or app folder. Review its contents.

rules.reason: Custom folder at drive root. Inspect before deciding.
rules.article: Not a Windows-standard folder. Could be a VirtualBox VM, project data, or download stash.

rules.reason: Game installs. Delete individual games you've finished playing.
rules.article: Game installs are large. Use each game's uninstaller; don't just delete folders.

rules.reason: Operating system. Use Disk Cleanup for safe reclaiming.
rules.article: Never delete this folder. Use Settings â†’ System â†’ Storage or cleanmgr for safe space recovery.

rules.reason: Installed applications. Uninstall via Settings â†’ Apps.
rules.article: Deleting an installed app's folder leaves registry entries and services orphaned. Use Settings â†’ Apps â†’ Uninstall.

rules.reason: Installed applications. Uninstall via Settings â†’ Apps.
rules.article: Same as Program Files, for 32-bit applications.

rules.reason: Windows recovery environment.
rules.article: Needed to repair or reset Windows. Never delete.

rules.reason: Windows virtual memory. Deleting it can prevent Windows from booting.
rules.article: Windows uses pagefile as overflow RAM. You can move it to another drive or resize it, but never delete it.

rules.reason: System restore points. Manage via 'vssadmin resize shadowstorage'.
rules.article: Windows keeps restore points here. Shrinking the shadow storage cap via vssadmin frees space safely.

rules.reason: ComfyUI AI models. Large but required if you use ComfyUI. Back up models-manifest.md first.
rules.article: ComfyUI's models folder is often 10-50 GB. If you use ComfyUI, don't delete - back up the models. If not, safe to remove.

rules.reason: VS Code extensions. Re-installable from your extensions list.
rules.article: Each extension is a folder here. Re-installable from Settings -> Extensions -> @installed.
